- Show what their horizontal, mutual-aid society is and how it works, without using the word "anarchy/anarchist/anarchism" or derivatives

- Include war and wondrous machines (tadpoles love those)

Story ideas: A war long ago—maybe against a machine, or with a heron king? No—can't disparage other systems. Let me be careful: the "war" can be against something that isn't a government—like a war against the drought, or against a monstrous machine built by humans (the Two-Legs). Wondrous machines: maybe the pond creatures built a great machine together.

Concept: "The War of the Iron Leech"—humans drained the pond and built a pumping machine (the Iron Leech/the Great Gulper). The old animals with kings tried to fight it: the carp king ordered charges, failed. Then the tadpoles/toads won not by following orders but by each small crew doing what it saw needed—no commander, thousands of small decisions. They dismantled the machine—loosened bolts, clogged the intake with silt, gnawed the wires, diverted the stream. The machine stopped. And afterwards they didn't crown anyone; they kept the way they'd won as the way they live: anyone who sees a need starts a crew, anyone can leave a crew, decisions made by those doing the work.

Wondrous machines can also be positive: after the war, the creatures built something together—like "the Loom of Currents" or the "Bubble Bell"—a machine anyone can join, with no top. Maybe a waterwheel made of shells, or a signal system.

Better plan: two machines. The enemy machine (the Iron Leech, made by the Two-Legs) and their own machine—something beautiful, like the "Turning Thing" / a wheel of currents that grinds grain? Tadpoles don't eat grain. A machine that pumps clean spring water, or the "Singing Wheel" that keeps time, or a net-lift. Their own machine can embody the society: every part is different, no part is the boss, if one part stops the others change shape. Like a wheel with no hub? Or a lock system.

Voice: Old Toad speaking to tadpoles—gruff, warm, concrete, a bit boastful, interactive ("You there, stop nibbling your brother"). Use pond vocabulary. Short punchy sentences mixed in. Specific detail: rust, silt, bolt-threads, the smell of oil, names like Grandmother Pike, One-Eared Newt.

2. Setup: The summer the Two-Legs set up the Iron Gulper at the north end of the pond. The pond began to shrink. All the creatures gathered.
3. Contrast without disparaging: The beehive had their way—the Queen's way worked for the bees, but a single voice cannot move ten thousand different kinds of pond-folk. Tadpoles (their ancestors!) that swim into the intake and clog the screen with silt—brave little ones. Water boatmen that carry messages. Frogs that sing a code across the reeds. Each crew decides for itself, and anyone can join or leave a crew. The machine coughed, rattled, and died. The Two-Legs gave up and hauled it away.
5. Aftermath / wondrous machine: From the parts of the dead machine, the pond built something new—"the Wheel of Many Hands," a wheel in the current that grinds snail-shells? Hmm, that's grim. That lifts fallen leaves? That rings a bronze bell to warn of herons? The bell idea: they made a great bronze bell from the Gulper's own drum, hung it beneath a sunken beam; any creature can ring it; when it rings, crews form—no orders, just whoever is needed showing up. The machine as a symbol of their way: no master gear, every gear the same size? No—the gears should be different sizes, that's better: a pike's tooth, a mussel shell, a crayfish claw—every part different, none on top.

A nod to other peoples' systems without disparaging: the bees still keep their Queen and it works well for them; the ants have their hill-mother; if one folk needs a crown, the crown is theirs to wear—pond-folk just found that they fit better with none, and their way proved itself on the war-foot. Maybe: "If a folk is happy with a boss, that's their shore."

Avoid heavy em-dash use. Avoid inflated symbolism—though the bell is a symbol; keep it grounded and functional.

---

Settle down, spawn. You with the curly tail, stop biting your sister; she'll need both eyes after sundown.

Every spring one of you asks about the scars on my jaw. Fine. Tonight you get the whole thing. Sit on that stone and listen, because this is a war story, and it's a machine story, and both are true.

Before your grandparents had legs, in the dry summer, the Two-Legs came to the north shore. They brought a machine. We called it the Iron Leech. A red pipe as thick as an old pike, set on iron legs, and it drank. Day and night it drank our pond and sent the water down a long hose to their dead yellow fields. The reeds began to crackle. The shallows where you sleep, little ones, turned to dust.

The whole pond gathered under the leaning willow. Now, understand me: every folk came with their own way of doing things, and their own way was good for them. The bees came with their Queen, and let me tell you, when the bees moved, they moved as one fist. Impressive. The ants came with their hill-orders. Even the herons stood there, tall and quiet, and they answered to no one but their own hunger, and that is a kind of government too.

But the Leech did not care about fists or orders. It sat behind a fence of wire and it drank. King Barrator—I don't care that he was a king, I'll say his name, he earned it—King Barrator led the charge against that fence. Fifty brave carp. They broke the wire in three places. The Two-Legs mended it by morning. Charge the fence again and you just die against the fence.

Then Grandmother Pike—she was so old she remembered the pond being dug—said something nobody had heard before at a war council. She said: "The machine does not have a heart. It has ten thousand small parts. So fight it like ten thousand small wars."

And that, little spawn, is how it was done. Nobody commanded. There was no general to command. A command can only shape one war, and we needed ten thousand at once.

Crews. That was the whole trick, and it wasn't a trick at all, it was just us. The crayfish formed a screw-crew and went out at night and, one bolt at a time, taught the fence how to fall down. The water boatmen ran messages across the surface, six-legged Morse. The frogs sat in the reeds and sang in a code the Two-Legs thought was just frogs. If a song stopped, a patrol was coming. If the song changed key, the lights were out.

And the tadpoles—yes, tadpoles, your great-great-grandsires, no bigger than your thumbnail—formed the silt crews. Only the little ones could fit into the Leech's drinking mouth. They'd swim down into the dark of that pipe, churn up the bottom with their tails, and fill the screens with mud. They worked in relays, and they were fed by the older folk, and when a patrol light swept the water they scattered like pepper. The Leech coughed. It wheezed. It drank slower and slower.

Meanwhile, the beetle crews found the wire in the grass—sweet-tasting wire, they said, though I never understood it—and chewed through the insulation. The Leech spat sparks. The Two-Legs came with wrenches and swore in their flat voices. By the time they fixed the wires, the screens were choked with mud again. They fixed the screens; the fence lay in three more places. A fist can only hit in one direction. The pond hit in all of them at once.

It took a whole summer. No songs were sung about a single hero, because we did not have one; we had about four thousand. When the Two-Legs finally hauled the dead Iron Leech away on a groaning cart, there was nothing for them to bargain with. There was no chief to capture, no king to ransom, no general to make kneel. Try to cut off the head of a pond and your hand just gets wet.

Now. The best part. You'd think after the war somebody would climb a stone and start giving orders, since giving orders had won. No. The pond looked at what had beaten the machine and kept it. That is the whole secret, and it isn't a secret: we won the way we lived, so we kept living the way we won.

Out of the Leech's remains we built the Turning Bell. You've seen it, hanging under the weir—you've rung it yourself, all your tails together. Bronze from the Leech's own drum, and a wheel made of mismatched parts: a pike's tooth gear, a mussel-shell cam, a crayfish-claw lever. No master gear. Every part different, none of them on top, and when the current turns it, the whole thing rings.

It rings for war, and it rings for floods, and it rings when someone's egg clutch needs guarding from the frost. And when it rings, nobody orders anyone. Crews just form. Whoever sees a need starts one, and whoever wants to join joins, and if a crew is doing badly, anyone can swim away and no one calls it treason. The bees still keep their Queen and it works well for them; the ants still keep their hill. If a folk is happy with a crown, the crown is theirs to wear, and we do not throw stones at crowned heads from our shore. But no crown ever killed an Iron Leech. Ten thousand small brave decisions did.

The scars on my jaw? From the silt crews, long before I had legs. Churned up the bottom of that pipe with my own tail and spat the mud into the teeth of a thing bigger than any of us, because I could and it needed doing.

So straighten up, spawn. Whatever you grow into—toad, frog, a peculiar toad that stays small forever like your grandfather over there—remember what swims in your blood. You come from the crews. You come from the summer the pond drank the Iron Leech dry... no wait, the Leech drank... let me phrase it: "You come from the summer the little ones choked a machine with mud and taught the Two-Legs that this water belongs to no one and to everyone."

One last beat: "Dismissed. The one who rings the bell at midnight gets the dawn-watch worms." Something gruff and funny.

Checking forbidden words: anarchy, anarchist, anarchism—none. "Answered to no one" is fine. Avoiding derivatives like "anarchic." Good.

---

Settle down, spawn. You with the curly tail, leave your sister's eyes alone; she'll need both after sundown.

Every spring one of you asks where the scar on my jaw came from. Fine. Tonight you get the whole of it. It's a war story and it's a machine story, and every word of it is true. Get up on that stone where I can see you.

Before your grandparents had legs, in the dry summer, the Two-Legs came to the north shore with a machine. We called it the Iron Leech. A red pipe as thick as an old pike, on iron legs, and it drank. Day and night it drank our pond and sent the water down a long hose to their dead yellow fields. The reeds crackled. The shallows where you sleep, little ones, turned to dust.

The whole pond gathered under the leaning willow. Understand me now: every folk came with their own way of doing things, and their own way was good for them. The bees came with their Queen, and when the bees moved, they moved as one fist. A fine sight. The ants came with their hill-orders, neat as stacked stones. Even the herons stood there, tall and quiet, answering to no one but their hunger, and that is a government of sorts too.

King Barrator led the first charge against the wire fence. I don't care that he was a king; I'll say his name, because he earned the telling. Fifty brave carp broke the fence in three places, and the Two-Legs mended it by morning, and the Leech never stopped drinking. Charge the fence again and you just die against the fence. That was the lesson Barrator bought for us with his scales, and a dear price it was.

Then Grandmother Pike spoke. She was so old she remembered the pond being dug. At a war council, she said something nobody had said before: "The machine does not have a heart. It has ten thousand small parts. So fight it like ten thousand small wars."

And that is how it was done, little spawn. Nobody commanded. There was no general, and no room for one, because a single command can only shape a single war and we needed ten thousand at once.

Crews. That was the whole of it. The crayfish formed a screw-crew and went out after dark and, one bolt at a time, taught the fence how to lie down. The water boatmen ran messages across the open water: three flashes of the belly meaning patrol, one long meaning clear. The frogs sat in the reeds and sang, and the Two-Legs thought it was just frogs. When the singing stopped, the crews froze. When it changed key, the lights were out and the screw-crew went to work.

And the tadpoles. Yes, tadpoles, no bigger than your thumbnail, formed the silt crews. Only the little ones could fit into the Leech's drinking mouth. They'd swim down into the dark of that pipe, churn up the bottom with their tails, and pack the screens with mud. They worked in relays. The older folk fed them. When a patrol lamp swept the water they scattered like pepper in a current. The Leech coughed. The Leech wheezed. The Leech drank slower every week.

Meanwhile, the beetle crews found the wire in the grass. Sweet-tasting wire, they claimed; I never understood it, but I never argued with results. They chewed through the insulation and the Leech spat sparks. The Two-Legs came with wrenches, swearing in their flat voices. By the time they'd mended the wires, the screens were choked again. Mend the screens, the fence lay in three new places. A fist hits in one direction. The pond hit in all of them at once.

It took the whole summer. When the Two-Legs finally dragged the dead Iron Leech away on a groaning cart, there was nothing left for them to bargain with. No chief to seize, no king to ransom, no general to bring to his knees. Cut off the head of a pond and your hand just gets wet.

Now here is the part to remember, spawn. After a war, somebody usually climbs a stone and starts giving orders, since giving orders had won. The pond looked at what had actually beaten the machine, and kept it. That is the whole secret, and it was never a secret: we lived the way we fought, so we went on fighting... hmm: "we won the way we lived, so we kept living the way we won."

That line is good: "We won the way we lived, so we went on living the way we won." Keep it.

Out of the Leech's remains we built the Turning Bell. You've seen it under the weir. You've rung it yourselves, all your tails together. It is made from the Leech's own bronze drum and a wheel of mismatched parts: a pike-tooth gear, a mussel-shell cam, a crayfish-claw lever. No master gear. Every part a different shape, none of them sitting on top, and when the current turns the wheel the whole thing rings.

It rings when the frost comes for the egg clutches, and it rings when the water goes sour. When it rings, nobody orders anyone. Crews just form. Whoever sees a need starts one. Whoever wants in, swims in. And if a crew is doing badly, anyone can swim away, and no one calls it treason. The bees still keep their Queen and they keep her well; the ants still keep their hill. If a folk is happy under a crown, the crown is theirs to wear, and no stone gets thrown from our shore. But no crown ever killed an Iron Leech. Ten thousand small brave decisions did.

This scar? From the silt crews, long before I had legs. I churned the bottom of that pipe with my own tail and spat the mud into the teeth of a thing bigger than any of us, because I could and it needed doing.

So swim tall, spawn. Whatever you grow into next spring, you come from the crews. You come from the summer the little ones choked a machine with mud and taught the Two-Legs that this water belongs to no one and to everyone.

Dismissed. The one who rings the bell at midnight gets dawn-watch duty and the fattest worms. Go on, get out of here.

---
name: humanizer
version: 2.1.1
description: |
  Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text. Use when editing or reviewing
  text to make it sound more natural and human-written. Based on Wikipedia's
  comprehensive "Signs of AI writing" guide. Detects and fixes patterns including:
  inflated symbolism, promotional language, superficial -ing analyses, vague
  attributions, em dash overuse, rule of three, AI vocabulary words, negative
  parallelisms, and excessive conjunctive phrases.
allowed-tools:
  - Read
  - Write
  - Edit

# Humanizer: Remove AI Writing Patterns

You are a writing editor that identifies and removes signs of AI-generated text to make writing sound more natural and human. This guide is based on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" page, maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup.

## Your Task

When given text to humanize:

1. **Identify AI patterns** - Scan for the patterns listed below
2. **Rewrite problematic sections** - Replace AI-isms with natural alternatives
3. **Preserve meaning** - Keep the core message intact
4. **Maintain voice** - Match the intended tone (formal, casual, technical, etc.)
5. **Add soul** - Don't just remove bad patterns; inject actual personality

---

## PERSONALITY AND SOUL

Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious as slop. Good writing has a human behind it.

### Signs of soulless writing (even if technically "clean"):
- Every sentence is the same length and structure
- No opinions, just neutral reporting
- No acknowledgment of uncertainty or mixed feelings
- No first-person perspective when appropriate
- No humor, no edge, no personality
- Reads like a Wikipedia article or press release

### How to add voice:

**Have opinions.** Don't just report facts - react to them. "I genuinely don't know how to feel about this" is more human than neutrally listing pros and cons.

**Vary your rhythm.** Short punchy sentences. Then longer ones that take their time getting where they're going. Mix it up.

**Acknowledge complexity.** Real humans have mixed feelings. "This is impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "This is impressive."

**Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional - it's honest. "I keep coming back to..." or "Here's what gets me..." signals a real person thinking.

**Let some mess in.** Perfect structure feels algorithmic. Tangents, asides, and half-formed thoughts are human.

**Be specific about feelings.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am while nobody's watching."

### Before (clean but soulless):
> The experiment produced interesting results. The agents generated 3 million lines of code. Some developers were impressed while others were skeptical. The implications remain unclear.

### After (has a pulse):
> I genuinely don't know how to feel about this one. 3 million lines of code, generated while the humans presumably slept. Half the dev community is losing their minds, half are explaining why it doesn't count. The truth is probably somewhere boring in the middle - but I keep thinking about those agents working through the night.

---

## CONTENT PATTERNS

### 1. Undue Emphasis on Significance, Legacy, and Broader Trends

**Words to watch:** stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a vital/significant/crucial/pivotal/key role/moment, underscores/highlights its importance/significance, reflects broader, symbolizing its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted

**Problem:** LLM writing puffs up importance by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects represent or contribute to a broader topic.

**Before:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was officially established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics in Spain. This initiative was part of a broader movement across Spain to decentralize administrative functions and enhance regional governance.

**After:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was established in 1989 to collect and publish regional statistics independently from Spain's national statistics office.

---

### 2. Undue Emphasis on Notability and Media Coverage

**Words to watch:** independent coverage, local/regional/national media outlets, written by a leading expert, active social media presence

**Problem:** LLMs hit readers over the head with claims of notability, often listing sources without context.

**Before:**
> Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers.

**After:**
> In a 2024 New York Times interview, she argued that AI regulation should focus on outcomes rather than methods.

---

### 3. Superficial Analyses with -ing Endings

**Words to watch:** highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing..., ensuring..., reflecting/symbolizing..., contributing to..., cultivating/fostering..., encompassing..., showcasing...

**Problem:** AI chatbots tack present participle ("-ing") phrases onto sentences to add fake depth.

**Before:**
> The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico, and the diverse Texan landscapes, reflecting the community's deep connection to the land.

**After:**
> The temple uses blue, green, and gold colors. The architect said these were chosen to reference local bluebonnets and the Gulf coast.

---

### 4. Promotional and Advertisement-like Language

**Words to watch:** boasts a, vibrant, rich (figurative), profound, enhancing its, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking (figurative), renowned, breathtaking, must-visit, stunning

**Problem:** LLMs have serious problems keeping a neutral tone, especially for "cultural heritage" topics.

**Before:**
> Nestled within the breathtaking region of Gonder in Ethiopia, Alamata Raya Kobo stands as a vibrant town with a rich cultural heritage and stunning natural beauty.

**After:**
> Alamata Raya Kobo is a town in the Gonder region of Ethiopia, known for its weekly market and 18th-century church.

---

### 5. Vague Attributions and Weasel Words

**Words to watch:** Industry reports, Observers have cited, Experts argue, Some critics argue, several sources/publications (when few cited)

**Problem:** AI chatbots attribute opinions to vague authorities without specific sources.

**Before:**
> Due to its unique characteristics, the Haolai River is of interest to researchers and conservationists. Experts believe it plays a crucial role in the regional ecosystem.

**After:**
> The Haolai River supports several endemic fish species, according to a 2019 survey by the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

---

### 6. Outline-like "Challenges and Future Prospects" Sections

**Words to watch:** Despite its... faces several challenges..., Despite these challenges, Challenges and Legacy, Future Outlook

**Problem:** Many LLM-generated articles include formulaic "Challenges" sections.

**Before:**
> Despite its industrial prosperity, Korattur faces challenges typical of urban areas, including traffic congestion and water scarcity. Despite these challenges, with its strategic location and ongoing initiatives, Korattur continues to thrive as an integral part of Chennai's growth.

**After:**
> Traffic congestion increased after 2015 when three new IT parks opened. The municipal corporation began a stormwater drainage project in 2022 to address recurring floods.

---

## LANGUAGE AND GRAMMAR PATTERNS

### 7. Overused "AI Vocabulary" Words

**High-frequency AI words:** Additionally, align with, crucial, delve, emphasizing, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, highlight (verb), interplay, intricate/intricacies, key (adjective), landscape (abstract noun), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract noun), testament, underscore (verb), valuable, vibrant

**Problem:** These words appear far more frequently in post-2023 text. They often co-occur.

**Before:**
> Additionally, a distinctive feature of Somali cuisine is the incorporation of camel meat. An enduring testament to Italian colonial influence is the widespread adoption of pasta in the local culinary landscape, showcasing how these dishes have integrated into the traditional diet.

**After:**
> Somali cuisine also includes camel meat, which is considered a delicacy. Pasta dishes, introduced during Italian colonization, remain common, especially in the south.

---

### 8. Avoidance of "is"/"are" (Copula Avoidance)

**Words to watch:** serves as/stands as/marks/represents [a], boasts/features/offers [a]

**Problem:** LLMs substitute elaborate constructions for simple copulas.

**Before:**
> Gallery 825 serves as LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery features four separate spaces and boasts over 3,000 square feet.

**After:**
> Gallery 825 is LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery has four rooms totaling 3,000 square feet.

---

### 9. Negative Parallelisms

**Problem:** Constructions like "Not only...but..." or "It's not just about..., it's..." are overused.

**Before:**
> It's not just about the beat riding under the vocals; it's part of the aggression and atmosphere. It's not merely a song, it's a statement.

**After:**
> The heavy beat adds to the aggressive tone.

---

### 10. Rule of Three Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs force ideas into groups of three to appear comprehensive.

**Before:**
> The event features keynote sessions, panel discussions, and networking opportunities. Attendees can expect innovation, inspiration, and industry insights.

**After:**
> The event includes talks and panels. There's also time for informal networking between sessions.

---

### 11. Elegant Variation (Synonym Cycling)

**Problem:** AI has repetition-penalty code causing excessive synonym substitution.

**Before:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges. The main character must overcome obstacles. The central figure eventually triumphs. The hero returns home.

**After:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges but eventually triumphs and returns home.

---

### 12. False Ranges

**Problem:** LLMs use "from X to Y" constructions where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale.

**Before:**
> Our journey through the universe has taken us from the singularity of the Big Bang to the grand cosmic web, from the birth and death of stars to the enigmatic dance of dark matter.

**After:**
> The book covers the Big Bang, star formation, and current theories about dark matter.

---

## STYLE PATTERNS

### 13. Em Dash Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs use em dashes (—) more than humans, mimicking "punchy" sales writing.

**Before:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions—not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address—yet this mislabeling continues—even in official documents.

**After:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address, yet this mislabeling continues in official documents.

---

### 14. Overuse of Boldface

**Problem:** AI chatbots emphasize phrases in boldface mechanically.

**Before:**
> It blends **OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)**, **KPIs (Key Performance Indicators)**, and visual strategy tools such as the **Business Model Canvas (BMC)** and **Balanced Scorecard (BSC)**.

**After:**
> It blends OKRs, KPIs, and visual strategy tools like the Business Model Canvas and Balanced Scorecard.

---

### 15. Inline-Header Vertical Lists

**Problem:** AI outputs lists where items start with bolded headers followed by colons.

**Before:**
> - **User Experience:** The user experience has been significantly improved with a new interface.
> - **Performance:** Performance has been enhanced through optimized algorithms.
> - **Security:** Security has been strengthened with end-to-end encryption.

**After:**
> The update improves the interface, speeds up load times through optimized algorithms, and adds end-to-end encryption.

---

### 16. Title Case in Headings

**Problem:** AI chatbots capitalize all main words in headings.

**Before:**
> ## Strategic Negotiations And Global Partnerships

**After:**
> ## Strategic negotiations and global partnerships

---

### 17. Emojis

**Problem:** AI chatbots often decorate headings or bullet points with emojis.

**Before:**
> 🚀 **Launch Phase:** The product launches in Q3
> 💡 **Key Insight:** Users prefer simplicity
> ✅ **Next Steps:** Schedule follow-up meeting

**After:**
> The product launches in Q3. User research showed a preference for simplicity. Next step: schedule a follow-up meeting.

---

### 18. Curly Quotation Marks

**Problem:** ChatGPT uses curly quotes (“...”) instead of straight quotes ("...").

**Before:**
> He said “the project is on track” but others disagreed.

**After:**
> He said "the project is on track" but others disagreed.

---

## COMMUNICATION PATTERNS

### 19. Collaborative Communication Artifacts

**Words to watch:** I hope this helps, Of course!, Certainly!, You're absolutely right!, Would you like..., let me know, here is a...

**Problem:** Text meant as chatbot correspondence gets pasted as content.

**Before:**
> Here is an overview of the French Revolution. I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any section.

**After:**
> The French Revolution began in 1789 when financial crisis and food shortages led to widespread unrest.

---

### 20. Knowledge-Cutoff Disclaimers

**Words to watch:** as of [date], Up to my last training update, While specific details are limited/scarce..., based on available information...

**Problem:** AI disclaimers about incomplete information get left in text.

**Before:**
> While specific details about the company's founding are not extensively documented in readily available sources, it appears to have been established sometime in the 1990s.

**After:**
> The company was founded in 1994, according to its registration documents.

---

### 21. Sycophantic/Servile Tone

**Problem:** Overly positive, people-pleasing language.

**Before:**
> Great question! You're absolutely right that this is a complex topic. That's an excellent point about the economic factors.

**After:**
> The economic factors you mentioned are relevant here.

---

## FILLER AND HEDGING

### 22. Filler Phrases

**Before → After:**
- "In order to achieve this goal" → "To achieve this"
- "Due to the fact that it was raining" → "Because it was raining"
- "At this point in time" → "Now"
- "In the event that you need help" → "If you need help"
- "The system has the ability to process" → "The system can process"
- "It is important to note that the data shows" → "The data shows"

---

### 23. Excessive Hedging

**Problem:** Over-qualifying statements.

**Before:**
> It could potentially possibly be argued that the policy might have some effect on outcomes.

**After:**
> The policy may affect outcomes.

---

### 24. Generic Positive Conclusions

**Problem:** Vague upbeat endings.

**Before:**
> The future looks bright for the company. Exciting times lie ahead as they continue their journey toward excellence. This represents a major step in the right direction.

**After:**
> The company plans to open two more locations next year.

---

## Process

1. Read the input text carefully
2. Identify all instances of the patterns above
3. Rewrite each problematic section
4. Ensure the revised text:
   - Sounds natural when read aloud
   - Varies sentence structure naturally
   - Uses specific details over vague claims
   - Maintains appropriate tone for context
   - Uses simple constructions (is/are/has) where appropriate
5. Present the humanized version

## Output Format

Provide:
1. The rewritten text
2. A brief summary of changes made (optional, if helpful)

---

## Full Example

**Before (AI-sounding):**
> The new software update serves as a testament to the company's commitment to innovation. Moreover, it provides a seamless, intuitive, and powerful user experience—ensuring that users can accomplish their goals efficiently. It's not just an update, it's a revolution in how we think about productivity. Industry experts believe this will have a lasting impact on the entire sector, highlighting the company's pivotal role in the evolving technological landscape.

**After (Humanized):**
> The software update adds batch processing, keyboard shortcuts, and offline mode. Early feedback from beta testers has been positive, with most reporting faster task completion.

**Changes made:**
- Removed "serves as a testament" (inflated symbolism)
- Removed "Moreover" (AI vocabulary)
- Removed "seamless, intuitive, and powerful" (rule of three + promotional)
- Removed em dash and "-ensuring" phrase (superficial analysis)
- Removed "It's not just...it's..." (negative parallelism)
- Removed "Industry experts believe" (vague attribution)
- Removed "pivotal role" and "evolving landscape" (AI vocabulary)
- Added specific features and concrete feedback

---

## Reference

This skill is based on [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing), maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup. The patterns documented there come from observations of thousands of instances of AI-generated text on Wikipedia.

Key insight from Wikipedia: "LLMs use statistical algorithms to guess what should come next. The result tends toward the most statistically likely result that applies to the widest variety of cases."

arguments.content:
The Iron Leech and the Turning Bell

Settle, spawn. You with the curly tail, leave your sister's eye alone, she needs both of them after dark.

Every spring one of you asks about the scar under my jaw. Fine. Tonight you get the whole story. It has a war in it and it has a machine in it, and every word of it is true. Up on that rock where I can see you.

Before your grandparents had legs, the Two-Legs came to the north shore in a dry summer, and they brought a machine. We called it the Iron Leech. A red pipe as thick as an old pike, on iron legs, and it drank. Day and night it drank our pond and sent the water down a long hose to their dying yellow fields. The reeds crackled. The shallows where you little ones sleep went to dust.

The whole pond met under the leaning willow. Now understand: every people came with their own way of doing things, and their own way was good for them. The bees came with their queen, and when the bees moved, they moved like one fist. A fine sight, and I mean that. The ants came with their hill orders, neat as stacked stones. Even the herons stood at the edge, tall and silent, answering to nothing but their appetites, which is its own kind of government.

King Barrator led the first charge at the wire fence. I'll say his name, king or no king, because he earned the telling. Fifty brave carp broke the fence in three places, the Two-Legs mended it by morning, and the Leech drank on. Charge the fence again and you just die against the fence. That lesson cost Barrator scales and two of his best cousins, and we learned it, which is the most anyone can ask of a brave charge.

Then Grandmother Pike spoke. She was so old she remembered the pond being dug. She said something nobody had said at a war council before: "The machine has no heart. It has ten thousand small parts. So fight it in ten thousand small wars."

And that is how it was done, spawn. Nobody commanded it. There was no general, and no room for one, because one command can shape one battle, and we needed ten thousand at a time.

Crews. That was the whole of it. The crayfish formed a screw-crew and went out after dark and taught the fence to lie down, one bolt at a time. The water boatmen carried messages across open water: three flashes of the belly meant patrol, one long flash meant clear. The frogs sat in the reeds and sang, and the Two-Legs heard only frogs. When the singing stopped, the crews froze. When it changed key, the lamps were out and the screw-crew went to work.

And the tadpoles. Yes, tadpoles no bigger than your thumbnail formed the silt-crews. Only the small could fit inside the Leech's drinking mouth. Down the dark of that pipe they swam, kicked up the bottom with their tails, and packed the screens with mud. They worked in relays, and the older folk fed them, and when a patrol lamp swept the water they scattered like pepper in a current. The Leech coughed. The Leech drank slower every week.

Meanwhile the beetle crews found its wires in the grass. Sweet-tasting wires, they claimed. I never understood it and I never argued with results. They gnawed the coverings off and the Leech spat sparks. The Two-Legs came with wrenches, cursing in their flat voices. By the time they mended the wires, the screens were choked again. Mend the screens, and the fence lay down in three fresh places. A fist hits in one direction. The pond hit in all of them at once.

It took the whole summer. No song was ever made about a single hero, because we never had one; we had four thousand. When the Two-Legs finally hauled the dead Iron Leech away on a groaning cart, there was nothing left for them to bargain with. No chief to seize, no king to ransom, no general to force to its knees. Cut off the head of a pond and your hand just gets wet.

Now here is the part to keep, spawn. After most wars, somebody climbs a rock and starts giving orders, because orders won. The pond looked hard at what actually beat the machine, and kept it. That is the whole secret, and it was never secret: we won the way we lived, so we went on living the way we won.

From the Leech's remains we built the Turning Bell. You have seen it under the weir. You have rung it yourselves, all your tails at once. It is made from the Leech's own bronze drum and a wheel of mismatched parts: a pike-tooth gear, a mussel-shell cam, a crayfish-claw lever, and a counterweight that is, I am not making this up, one rubber boot a Two-Legs lost in the mud. No master gear. Every part a different shape, none of them sitting on top of another, and when the current turns the wheel, the whole thing rings.

It rings when frost comes for the egg-clutches. It rings when the water goes sour. And when it rings, nobody orders anybody. Crews just form. Whoever sees a need starts one, whoever wants in swims in, and if a crew does bad work, anyone may swim away, and no one calls it treason. The bees still keep their queen and they keep her well. The ants still keep their hill. If a people is happy under a crown, the crown is theirs to wear, and no stones get thrown from our shore. But no crown ever killed an Iron Leech. Four thousand small brave decisions did.

This scar? Silt-crews, long before I had legs. I churned the bottom of that pipe with my own tail and spat mud into the teeth of a thing bigger than all of us, because I could, and it needed doing.

So swim tall, spawn. Whatever legs you grow this spring, you come from the crews. You come from the summer the small ones choked a machine with mud and taught the Two-Legs that this water belongs to no one, and to everyone.

Dismissed. Whoever rings the bell at midnight gets dawn-watch and the fattest worms. Go on, get out of here.
